Phil's Motion Shelf

1487 prompts, films, styles, skills and blocks from 25 code-animation sources. Start with Top picks: the most-liked new prompts, each with its original video. 1004 have their original video right on the card: hover a card to play it, move away to stop. Open "Full prompt" to read or copy it.

Filmmg-styles-15

Frame-by-Frame

Hand-drawn frame by frame, or frame-by-frame texture laid over vector animation. Its signature is line boil: the lines jitter slightly every few frames, as if the picture were breathing. Studios such as Giant Ant and Buck dress their main animation with cel elements (smoke, splashes, speed lines); it is the core antidote to digital polish.

Filmmg-styles-15

Isometric 2.5D

A miniature world in 30° isometric projection: small cities, office cutaways, server rooms, with no vanishing point and everything at one scale. Dense with information yet cute, it is the standard look for tech architecture animations and app feature demos. School of Motion has a whole isometric mograph tutorial series.

Filmmg-styles-15

Flat Vector

The mainstream baseline of motion graphics, from the Google Material and corporate explainer tradition: geometric characters and scenes in flat colour, no or minimal outlines, bold colour blocks, every element a vector shape. Common in SaaS promos, science explainers and annual-report videos.

1920×108010 s
Full prompt

Filmmg-styles-15

Line Art

A thin single-colour line is the only visual language: it draws itself on, extends, turns and morphs into the next shape, the whole film in one stroke. Minimal and premium, common in luxury, finance and architecture brand films and logo animations.

1920×108010 s
Full prompt

Filmmg-styles-15

3D Render

Solid, tactile animation rendered in Cinema 4D with Redshift/Octane, or in Blender: soft rubber, glass, metal, cloth, with cloner arrays and physics simulation. The mainstream look for high-end product films (phones, drinks, sneakers) and brand idents; Maxon's official demo reel sets the trend each year.

1920×108010 s
Full prompt

Filmmg-styles-15

Shape Morph

One shape turns smoothly and continuously into another: a phone becomes a map pin, a coffee cup becomes a sunset. It is the core grammar of visual storytelling, and the most skilful part of Apple keynote motion and high-end explainers.

1920×108010 s
Full prompt
Source
Filmmg-styles-15

Sticker Explainer

The standard package of Chinese knowledge videos, made popular by PaperClip (回形针): photos are cut out and given a thick white outline to become stickers, laid out with flat icons and data charts on a huge canvas, while the camera pans and zooms from point to point. Finance and cross-disciplinary creators such as Lin Chao combine it with handwritten notes and formula cards. It is still the dominant format for hard-science, finance and corporate explainers.

Full prompt

Filmmg-styles-15

Cyberpunk HUD

Packaging that imitates the head-up displays of sci-fi films and games: cyan and orange neon wireframes, target-lock boxes, radar sweeps, streams of tiny data. It is the default skin for "tech" in gadget reviews, game edits (Cyberpunk 2077, Evangelion fan edits), military and space explainers and AI product demos; AE HUD tutorials on Bilibili reach 200,000 views.

Filmmg-styles-15

Collage

A retro, surreal style that cuts up old photos, newspapers and torn paper and reassembles them, rooted in Monty Python and Soviet constructivist posters. Hallmarks: unbalanced head-to-body proportions, mouths that open on their own, halftone textures. Lately merged with the magazine look, it is a frequent choice for music and streetwear short videos.

Filmmg-styles-15

Aurora & Glassmorphism

Large, heavily blurred colour blobs (aurora / mesh gradient) drift slowly underneath, with frosted translucent glass cards floating on top. Apple's iOS 26 Liquid Glass and a wave of AI product launches made it the default look of tech brand films in 2024–2026: slow, translucent, premium.

1920×108010 s
Full prompt
Source
Filmmg-styles-15

Geometric Bauhaus

Circles, triangles and rectangles move, rotate and scale precisely on a strict grid, in a limited palette of the three primaries plus black and white: the ordered beauty of machine rationality. It comes from the Bauhaus and the Swiss International graphic tradition (Adobe once worked with the Bauhaus archive on the Hidden Treasures project), and it is the main language of kinetic posters, a natural match for musical beats.

1920×108010 s
Full prompt
Source
Filmmg-styles-15

80s Synthwave

A wholesale quotation of one era's media aesthetics: 80s synthwave is neon grids, sunset gradients and chrome type; VHS is scanlines, colour shift and tape noise; Y2K is liquid chrome, acid green and purple, skeuomorphic system windows and lo-fi 3D. Y2K has come back strongly in music videos and fashion brand films over the last two years, and Bilibili's template market is full of "acid chrome" assets.

Filmmg-styles-15

Pixel Art

Retro game aesthetics: low resolution with big pixels, a limited palette and low-frame-rate sprite animation. Common in Bilibili's game section (Minecraft, Terraria, indie games), 8-bit music videos and nostalgic brand marketing; Aseprite tutorials on Bilibili draw 100,000+ views in a steady learning community.

Filmmg-styles-15

Liquid Motion

Shapes flow, stretch into strings, drip and merge like liquid: a transition is a splash of paint washing over the screen, a logo gathers itself out of a single drop. Organic, satisfying and high-energy, widely used in music videos, food and drink ads and transition packages.

Filmmg-styles-15

Variety Captions

Emotional decorative captions from TV variety-show post-production: rounded type with several outline layers springs in, changes colour and shape with the person's mood, and comes with hit sound effects. Now the everyday packaging of vlogs, pet videos, interviews and comedy edits; CapCut ships many caption templates, and free caption packs circulate on Bilibili.

Styleanimate

Isometric line art

Calm, precise product illustration: objects in 2:1 dimetric isometric on a white ground, drawn only with constant hairlines. Grey silhouettes and edges, lighter inner and receding lines, faces filled white so nearer objects hide farther lines. Rounded slabs and plates with visible thickness, stacked layers, grids of repeated parts (keys, vents, pillars, ports), and one tiny dark accent per frame. Motion on 1s with spring settles; otherwise still. Studied from MIT-licensed isometric line figures (references kept local, never copied).

Styleanimate

Pixel

Pixel art. Every picture is drawn at a low internal resolution — 90x160, 135x240, 180x320 for a 9:16 frame — with whole-pixel primitives in a limited palette, then scaled up nearest-neighbour to 1080x1920. Hard square pixels, ordered (Bayer) dithering instead of gradients, a built-in 5x7 bitmap font, sprites from string arrays, and screen effects that belong to a device: an LCD grid for a handheld, scanlines and a curved-tube vignette for an arcade. **Resolution can tell time:** an early era is chunkier than a later one, so a chronology gets sharper as it goes.
